strengths: The core idea—learning a targeted, one-dimensional representation from factual and counterfactual parameter gradients—is intuitive, technically interesting, and potentially useful beyond gender debiasing.
The empirical study has unusually broad architectural coverage, spanning seven encoder-only and decoder-only models, including BERT, RoBERTa, GPT-2, and LLaMA variants.
The paper compares against numerous established debiasing methods and evaluates both bias and utility using StereoSet, SEAT, CrowS-Pairs, GLUE, and a separate language-modeling measure.

The appendix provides substantial implementation detail, per-model results, confidence intervals, dataset construction procedures, computational requirements, and an explicit discussion of some limitations.
The presentation is generally clear and polished, and the parameter-grid visualizations make the behavior of the learned update direction relatively easy to understand.
weaknesses: The central claim of learning a monosemantic feature is not established. A scalar bottleneck is forced to discriminate gradients constructed from explicitly gender-labeled names and he/she targets, so strong performance on closely related gender-prediction tasks demonstrates supervised separability, not monosemanticity. The method is also described as unsupervised despite relying on gender labels, curated gendered pronouns, and factual/counterfactual supervision.

A crucial ablation is missing. Since dec(h)=hWd+bd, the decoder bias alone supplies an update even when h=0; indeed, the selected BERT-base debiasing configuration uses h=0. Thus, part of the main result may reduce to learning an average gradient update rather than using the claimed feature neuron. Comparisons against bd alone, the mean gradient difference, rank-one SVD/PCA directions, and direct optimization are needed.

The evidence for selectivity is weak. Neutral examples come from heavily filtered, related data and merely use different prediction targets. There are no evaluations showing that the scalar is insensitive to correlated attributes, names versus gender, syntax, token frequency, or other semantic concepts, nor causal tests showing that the encoder value itself is responsible for debiasing.

The headline state-of-the-art conclusion rests mainly on a proportional-rank aggregation. Ranking discards effect magnitude and uncertainty, gives equal weight to heterogeneous metrics, and is not accompanied by statistical testing of the aggregate. Many apparent differences from INLP or SENT-DEBIAS fall within the reported confidence intervals. Table 4's utility values also appear to reproduce the BERT-base values rather than averages across the seven base models, despite the caption describing mean changes, creating a material reporting inconsistency.

Only the best of three GRADIEND runs is retained according to validation correlation, while downstream results do not quantify variation across GRADIEND training seeds. Bootstrap intervals over benchmark examples do not capture this training and model-selection variance. Statistical significance is inferred from non-overlapping marginal confidence intervals rather than paired tests, with no correction for the very large number of comparisons.

Hyperparameters h and alpha are selected through an extensive grid on the authors' custom GENTYPES metric. This 500-example benchmark was generated iteratively by GPT-4o, manually filtered, and exhibits acknowledged artifacts such as an unexpected RoBERTa gender direction. Conclusions based on BPI/FPI/MPI therefore risk selection overfitting and depend strongly on an insufficiently validated metric.

The practical method is extremely expensive: it introduces roughly three additional parameters per modified base-model parameter and requires repeated full-model gradients, up to two 80GB A100 GPUs and hundreds of gigabytes for validation gradients. The paper does not compare compute, memory, or parameter efficiency against baselines, substantially limiting the claimed broad applicability.

Reproducibility is incomplete in the submitted manuscript: the dataset and model identifier tables are blank, the stated public implementation has no visible URL, and the GPT-4o dataset-generation citation is missing. Some baseline settings are transferred to unsupported architectures without validation, and GLUE is evaluated under incomparable fine-tuned and zero-shot protocols across model families.

The ethical discussion acknowledges binary gender and misuse risks but does not adequately address misgendering, the demographic limitations of name-derived gender labels, intersectional bias, or safeguards for releasing deliberately gender-amplified models.

strengths: The core idea—learning a low-dimensional, gradient-derived direction for targeted model editing—is interesting and potentially useful.
The evaluation spans seven transformer variants, including encoder-only, decoder-only, and instruction-tuned models.
The paper compares against numerous debiasing baselines and evaluates both bias and utility using StereoSet, SEAT, CrowS-Pairs, GLUE, and bootstrapped confidence intervals.

The method and experimental motivation are generally understandable, with substantial supplementary results. weaknesses: The central monosemanticity claim is unsupported. The experiments show that one scalar can classify gender on a highly structured pronoun-gradient task, but do not establish that the neuron represents gender exclusively rather than names, pronoun identity, grammatical correlations, or other features. No causal interpretability tests, concept-purity analysis, or competing-feature controls are provided.

The claimed unsupervised learning is misleading: training explicitly uses gender-labeled names, factual gendered pronouns, and counterfactual pronouns. Near-perfect accuracy on held-out samples generated through the same pipeline is therefore largely circular and does not by itself demonstrate discovery of an interpretable feature.

The strongest debiasing claim rests on proportional ranks that discard effect magnitudes and uncertainty. Tiny, statistically inconclusive differences can change ranks as much as substantive improvements, while raw tables show mixed results across models and metrics. There is no statistical analysis of the aggregated ranking or convincing evidence that GRADIEND+INLP consistently improves over INLP.

Baseline parity is weak. GRADIEND receives a 15-by-16 per-model search over gender factors and learning rates using a custom selection metric, whereas several baselines use fixed or borrowed hyperparameters, including adaptations to architectures for which they were not originally configured. Some methods are also unavailable on LLaMA, making the cross-model rank aggregation insufficiently specified and potentially incomparable.

The assertion that other capabilities are maintained is too strong. Individual results include material, sometimes statistically significant utility losses—for example, GPT-2 GRADIENDBPI loses about 2.36 StereoSet language-modeling points and 2.89 GLUE points, while RoBERTa loses about 2.50 GLUE points. Averaging these effects across architectures obscures important failures.

The custom GENTYPES metric is based on GPT-4o-generated stereotypes and is used to select the final edit. Its construct validity is not established, and some selected models only marginally improve BPI. The method also readily creates extremely gender-polarized models, showing that it may manipulate name/pronoun associations rather than remove broader harmful stereotypes.

Essential ablations are missing: direct averaged factual/counterfactual gradient updates, a rank-one gradient baseline without an encoder, random or PCA/SVD directions, decoder-bias-only editing, parameter-matched alternatives, training-data-size sensitivity, and selection-grid robustness. Without them, it is unclear whether the proposed encoder-decoder contributes beyond extracting an obvious supervised gradient direction.

The work only studies binary English gender and explicitly trains models that amplify gender associations. Although acknowledged, the ethical discussion provides little analysis of downstream harms, intersectionality, non-binary identities, or safeguards for releasing deliberately biased checkpoints.

strengths: GRADIEND is a clear and interesting method: a one-dimensional bottleneck learns from factual versus counterfactual gradients and yields a reusable parameter-update direction for controlling gender associations.

The empirical scope is unusually broad, covering seven encoder- and decoder-based models, multiple model scales, three established bias benchmarks, GLUE/language-modeling utility measures, and numerous debiasing baselines and combinations.

The strongest configuration, GRADIEND combined with INLP, obtains the best aggregate bias rank while largely preserving measured language capabilities, providing concrete evidence that the learned update can complement representation-level debiasing.

The paper includes useful uncertainty estimates, detailed per-model results, hyperparameters, computational requirements, additional generalization analyses, and commitments to release datasets, code, and model checkpoints.
The presentation is generally clear, and the limitations and ethical section acknowledge binary-gender simplification and the risks of deliberately amplifying associations.
weaknesses: The claim of learning a “monosemantic” feature is stronger than the evidence. High gender classification accuracy on gradients produced from explicitly gender-labeled name/pronoun tasks establishes decodability, but not that the scalar represents gender exclusively rather than correlated properties of the constructed task. Broader semantic probes, counterexamples, and causal specificity tests are needed.

The approach is described as unsupervised, although construction of factual and counterfactual targets relies directly on known gender labels, gendered pronouns, curated gender-word lists, and gender-labeled names. It is more accurately characterized as targeted weakly supervised feature learning.

GRADIEND alone provides inconsistent and sometimes modest gains on standard bias benchmarks; several improvements overlap the reported confidence intervals, and some variants noticeably reduce language-modeling or GLUE performance. Much of the headline state-of-the-art result comes from combining GRADIEND with the already effective INLP method.

The aggregate proportional-rank analysis discards effect magnitudes and uncertainty and can amplify small, statistically inconclusive differences. Non-overlap of marginal confidence intervals is also not an ideal significance test; paired bootstrap tests with multiplicity control would support the comparative claims more convincingly.

Model selection depends on a bespoke GPT-4o-generated GENTYPES dataset and a fairly large grid over update factors and learning rates. The paper does not establish robustness of these choices across alternative selection datasets, and it explicitly reports convergence and parameter-selection instability.

The fairness scope remains narrow: binary gender is inferred primarily from first names and pronouns, with no evaluation of nonbinary identities, intersectional effects, downstream allocation harms, or whether legitimate gender information is unnecessarily erased. Intrinsic benchmark improvements alone do not establish socially meaningful debiasing.

strengths: The paper presents an interesting targeted gradient autoencoder that produces both a scalar class-related representation and a parameter-update direction, connecting feature analysis with model editing.

The empirical scope is unusually broad: seven transformer variants, encoder- and decoder-only architectures, three bias categories, established bias benchmarks, and GLUE/SuperGLUE capability evaluations.

The gender experiments provide reasonably consistent evidence that the learned scalar separates the constructed classes and that the decoder can controllably alter model behavior. Combining GRADIEND with INLP performs strongly on the reported gender-bias metrics.

The appendix provides substantial implementation, dataset, model-selection, uncertainty, and per-model result details. Confidence intervals, multiple downstream tasks, released code/models, and explicit limitations improve reproducibility and transparency.
The authors acknowledge binary and otherwise simplified social categories, the possibility of deliberate bias amplification, noisy race/religion data, and limitations for multi-token targets.
weaknesses: The central interpretation claim is overstated. GRADIEND is trained using explicitly constructed factual/counterfactual class targets, so describing the feature as learned "unsupervised" is inaccurate. Separating gradients from these supervised token-prediction tasks does not establish that the scalar is a monosemantic feature inside the original network.

Critical simple baselines and ablations are missing. The learned decoder should be compared with mean gradient differences, direct averaged-gradient updates, PCA/SVD directions, linear probes, and ordinary low-rank or one-step fine-tuning. Ablations of gradient differencing, the encoder, the decoder bias, and the one-dimensional bottleneck are needed to show what GRADIEND contributes beyond learning an affine gradient direction.

The claimed state-of-the-art debiasing result relies heavily on a custom proportional-rank aggregation and on combining GRADIEND with an existing method. Absolute improvements for GRADIEND alone are modest and inconsistent, while the leading gender combination reduces GLUE/SuperGLUE performance. Comparisons also mix fine-tuned and zero-shot protocols and sometimes different available model/method sets, weakening the aggregate ranking.

Evidence for race and religion is substantially weaker: no method improves SEAT significantly, the base model is competitive or superior on aggregate race results, some GRADIEND variants cause large language-modeling and downstream losses, and each model addresses only one pairwise axis. These results do not support broad claims of reliable debiasing.

Model selection uses bespoke scores and a GPT-4o-generated stereotype dataset whose validity is not independently established. For race and religion, selection reuses the test split of the constructed feature dataset, and the paper does not clearly separate all hyperparameter-selection data from final reporting. Results over the 15-by-16 editing grid therefore need stronger held-out validation.

The method is extremely expensive and poorly scalable: it introduces 3n+1 trainable parameters for n edited parameters, requires two model forward/backward passes per step, stores hundreds of gigabytes of validation gradients, and takes up to 24 hours on three 80GB A100s. Evaluation stops at 3B parameters, despite broader applicability claims.

The fairness framing remains narrow. Gender is inferred from names and reduced to a binary label, while race and religion are represented through noisy lexical substitutions. Standard intrinsic bias scores do not demonstrate improved fairness in consequential downstream settings, and the ethical discussion gives limited attention to cultural coverage, misgendering, intersectionality, or safeguards against the demonstrated bias-amplification capability.

strengths: The paper presents an interesting and conceptually simple idea: learning a one-dimensional bottleneck over parameter gradients and using its decoder as a model-editing direction. :codex-file-citation{path="/fsx/homes/Yaochen.Wang@mbzuai.ac.ae/AI-reviewer/res/review_iclr2026_yao_medium_20260919T2254Z/scratch/604f95225f7d40549674281869069528/work/manuscript.pdf" purpose="source"}
The empirical study covers seven transformer models, encoder- and decoder-only architectures, three bias categories, numerous debiasing baselines, and both GLUE and SuperGLUE.

The appendix provides substantial implementation and dataset detail, per-model results, bootstrap confidence intervals, an overfitting analysis, and explicit discussion of several limitations and ethical risks.
For some gender experiments, GRADIEND changes external bias metrics without severely degrading language-modeling or downstream-task performance.
weaknesses: The feature-learning evidence is substantially circular. Encoder inputs are gradients computed after supplying a class-specific target such as “he” or “she”; consequently, the target class is already directly embedded in the supervised gradient signal. Separating those gradients does not establish discovery of a semantic feature in ordinary model representations. Calling the procedure “unsupervised” is particularly misleading.

The central encoder-decoder interpretation lacks essential ablations. There is no comparison against an averaged gradient-difference update, direct optimization of one update vector, PCA or a linear probe, or decoder-only variants. Reconstruction error or explained variance is not reported. Most notably, the selected BERT-base gender intervention uses h=0, so its update is solely the decoder bias b_d; this directly undermines the claim that the learned feature neuron enables the edit.

The custom model-selection process searches 240 combinations of h and learning rate using BalancedBS, which is built from the same narrowly constructed task distribution. For gender, this relies on a GPT-4o-generated collection of only 500 stereotype templates; for race and religion, it reuses T-style data. There is no nested held-out set or correction for extensive configuration selection.

Table 7 is deeply concerning: for every displayed race/religion configuration, the base and modified probabilities P(A) and P(B) are identical to the reported precision, even when the paper claims meaningful debiasing. This either indicates that the selection metric detects essentially no relevant change or points to a reporting/implementation error.

The headline state-of-the-art claim is not supported convincingly. GRADIEND alone ranks ninth for gender and only narrowly exceeds CDA under the authors’ bespoke proportional-rank aggregation. The top result combines GRADIEND with INLP, but there is no factorial analysis showing that the improvement is attributable robustly to GRADIEND. For race and religion, results are inconsistent, the base model often ranks competitively, no method significantly improves SEAT, and some variants severely damage language modeling.

The proportional-rank aggregate discards effect sizes, uncertainty, and absolute distance from the unbiased target; it also depends on the set of methods being ranked and accommodates missing metrics unevenly. No confidence interval or significance analysis is provided for the aggregate on which the main comparative claims rest.

Training stability is insufficiently characterized. Gender runs sometimes fail to converge and the best of three seeds is selected, whereas race and religion use only one run. Reporting only selected runs and grid-optimal interventions prevents assessment of variance and robustness.

The method is extremely resource-intensive—gradient tensors can require hundreds of gigabytes and training uses up to three 80 GB A100 GPUs—yet it is compared insufficiently against much simpler gradient-based interventions. Together with the missing ablations, this leaves the practical and scientific value over direct supervised editing unclear.

strengths: GRADIEND is a creative and conceptually simple approach: a one-dimensional bottleneck learns from model gradients and its decoder produces parameter-space edits associated with a targeted feature.

The empirical scope is unusually broad, covering seven transformer models, encoder- and decoder-only architectures, three bias categories, multiple intrinsic bias metrics, language-modeling measurements, and GLUE/SuperGLUE evaluations.

The gender experiments provide meaningful positive evidence. Encoder values separate the target classes, edits can strongly control gender-associated predictions, and GRADIEND is competitive with other weight-modification methods while combining effectively with INLP.
The paper evaluates neutral inputs and classes unseen by particular pairwise models, providing some evidence beyond mere training-set reconstruction.
Comparisons include numerous relevant debiasing baselines and combinations. Bootstrap confidence intervals and multi-seed downstream evaluations improve the rigor of the empirical analysis.
The exposition is generally clear, the datasets and hyperparameters are described in substantial detail, and the authors report limitations and potential misuse of bias-amplifying edits.
weaknesses: The feature-learning claim lacks essential simple baselines and ablations. Because the decoder is linear and the encoder often saturates near plus or minus one, GRADIEND may primarily learn two class-conditioned prototype gradients. Comparisons against averaged gradient differences, direct task-vector updates, PCA/SVD, linear discriminants, and ordinary fine-tuning are needed to establish that the autoencoder and its learned neuron add value.

The evidence that the scalar represents a semantic feature rather than target-token or dataset identity is incomplete. Training and most encoder evaluations use closely related token-prediction constructions, while assigning neutral examples a desired label of zero does not independently validate interpretability. More out-of-domain, paraphrased, adversarial, and token-disjoint tests are needed.

Results outside binary gender are weak. The paper acknowledges that no method significantly improves race or religion SEAT, and the base model outperforms all race-debiasing methods on average. Table 7 additionally shows the selected race/religion edits leaving the reported class probabilities unchanged at the displayed precision in nearly every case, substantially weakening support for the broad H2 claim.

The headline state-of-the-art framing is stronger than the evidence. Standalone gender GRADIEND ranks only narrowly above CDA among weight-editing methods, whereas its strongest result comes from combination with INLP. The proportional-rank aggregation discards effect magnitudes and uncertainty and may be sensitive to the chosen model/metric set.

Model selection searches 240 feature-factor/learning-rate combinations using a bespoke BalancedBS objective. Stability to the grid, held-out selection data, alternative objectives, and random seeds is not adequately established; race and religion use only one training seed, while gender explicitly exhibits non-convergent runs and selects the best of three.

The method is expensive and poorly scaled: it introduces roughly three trainable parameters per edited base-model parameter, requires hundreds of gigabytes for cached evaluation gradients, and is demonstrated only up to 3B parameters. There is no comparison of compute, memory, or quality-efficiency against simpler editing approaches.

Preservation of general capabilities is not fully demonstrated. Fine-tuning on GLUE/SuperGLUE can obscure damage from the edit, several variants reduce intrinsic language-modeling scores, and broader zero-shot, generation-quality, factuality, and safety evaluations are absent.

The social-bias formulation is highly reductive, relying on binary gender and pairwise race/religion axes. Although acknowledged, this restricts the practical significance of the debiasing conclusions.
